title: The Sharpe Pint

opening_mood.text: Happy Friday. If you are looking across the pond today, you will find Wall Street completely dark as the Americans take an early long weekend for the 4th of July. That leaves the City to carry the torch, and there is plenty to chew on over your morning flat white. From Sam Altman trying to buy off the White House with a 5% equity tribute, to Mark Zuckerberg plotting a cloud side hustle, and a massive NBER takedown of the private credit boom, we have got you covered. Grab a coffee, and let's get sharp.

content.text: Here is your morning briefing on the key stories driving the City and global markets today, from political plays in AI to macro shifts and big-ticket private equity consolidation.
1. OpenAI Proposes Handing Trump Administration a 5% Stake

OpenAI has initiated early-stage, conceptual discussions about giving the US government a 5% equity stake in the company. Based on its recent $852 billion valuation, that slice would be worth roughly $42.6 billion. CEO Sam Altman has pitched the idea directly to President Donald Trump, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, arguing that public ownership is the fairest way to distribute the financial upside of artificial intelligence. Altman's proposal also suggests that other leading US AI developers, such as Anthropic, Google, and Meta, should pool similar 5% stakes into a sovereign wealth fund modeled on Alaska's oil-wealth Permanent Fund.

AI labs are facing intense political pressure in Washington over massive data centre energy consumption, job displacement, and national security. Anthropic recently had its latest model release temporarily held up by government security concerns. Handing over equity is a strategic move to secure political buy-in, smooth relations with a Trump administration that favors tighter regulation of the sector, and clear regulatory hurdles ahead of planned public listings.

For venture capitalists and asset managers, this raises massive questions about dilution, state intervention, and market competition. If the US government holds a direct equity stake in OpenAI, it completely alters the antitrust landscape and government procurement dynamics, potentially creating a state-sanctioned monopoly.

items: What to say in an interview: Altman's 5% proposal is a masterclass in regulatory capture disguised as public philanthropy. If the Trump administration takes the bait, OpenAI secures a massive political moat, but it sets a worrying precedent of 'equity for permission' that could spread to other highly regulated sectors.

What to say to colleagues: It's essentially a modern-day corporate tribute. If other tech giants refuse to play along, OpenAI could position itself as the 'national champion,' leaving rivals like Google and Meta in a tough spot politically.

content.text: 2. Meta Plots a Cloud Side Hustle to Recoup its AI Billions

Meta is developing plans for a new cloud infrastructure business, internally dubbed 'Meta Compute,' aimed at selling its excess AI computing capacity and hosted AI models to external developers. The company is exploring two service models: renting out raw GPU capacity (competing with specialized 'neocloud' providers like CoreWeave) and selling access to hosted AI models (similar to AWS's Bedrock). This comes as Meta's projected AI infrastructure capital expenditure for 2026 sits at an eye-watering $125 billion to $145 billion.

Up until now, Meta has been a massive consumer of AI hardware, not a seller. The news that Mark Zuckerberg might start renting out spare GPUs sent AI chip stocks tumbling globally, as traders panicked about a looming capacity glut. If Meta starts dumping excess compute onto the market, the pricing power of specialized GPU clouds and even Nvidia's hardware demand curve could take a hit.

For tech analysts, this is a classic 'monetise the overbuild' strategy. Zuckerberg admitted that companies approach Meta weekly asking to buy spare compute. If Meta can offset its massive capex by renting out its infrastructure, it changes the ROI calculations for its AI spend. But for markets, it's a signal that the initial 'scarcity' phase of the AI infrastructure boom is ending.

items: What to say in an interview: Meta entering the cloud space is a massive narrative shift. It suggests they've built more capacity than they can actually use for consumer products. While it helps Meta recoup some of its insane capex, it's a warning shot for Nvidia and specialized GPU renters like CoreWeave.

What to say to colleagues: The pick-and-shovel phase of the AI trade is getting incredibly crowded. If hyperscalers start competing on raw compute pricing, the margins for specialized AI cloud providers are going to collapse.

content.text: 3. US June Jobs Report Misses the Mark as Hiring Cools

US nonfarm payrolls for June rose by just 57,000, a massive miss against the consensus forecast of 115,000. Slower hiring was accompanied by downward revisions of 74,000 for April and May. Interestingly, the unemployment rate edged down slightly to 4.2% from 4.3%, but the overall picture is one of a cooling labor market.

The Federal Reserve has been keeping rates 'higher for longer' on the back of a resilient labor market. This soft print gives the FOMC clear evidence that the economy is cooling down, prompting traders to trim bets on any potential rate hikes later this month and boosting expectations for rate cuts later in the year.

Bond yields fell and the Dow closed at an all-time high ahead of the July 4th holiday weekend as bad economic news became good news for equity markets. For macro funds, the focus shifts from inflation-fighting to growth-preservation. It's a classic 'soft landing' indicator, but if hiring continues to decelerate at this pace, recession fears might start creeping back into the narrative.

items: What to say in an interview: The 57k print is a clear sign the US labor market is finally losing its post-pandemic steam. It takes any lingering rate hike fears off the table for the Fed and sets up a pivot. The equity market's positive reaction shows Wall Street is still in 'bad news is good news' mode.

What to say to colleagues: Keep an eye on the downward revisions. Losing 74k jobs from previous months suggests the labor market has been softer than we thought for a while. If the Fed doesn't cut soon, they risk falling behind the curve.

content.text: 4. Oil Tumbles to Four-Month Low as US-Iran Doha Talks Advance

Brent crude fell to around $70.50 a barrel and WTI dropped to $67.50, hitting their lowest levels since before the US-Iran conflict flared up in February. The drop followed news from Qatari and Pakistani mediators that indirect peace talks between the US and Iran in Doha made 'positive progress' on implementing the memorandum of understanding that halted the war in June.

The Strait of Hormuz, which handles a fifth of global oil supply, is seeing recovering traffic, with tankers previously stranded in the Gulf finally exporting crude. UBS cut its Brent price forecasts for the second half of 2026 to $80 a barrel (down $25 for Q3) citing the reopening of the strait.

For commodities desks and macro traders, the geopolitical risk premium is evaporating fast. The 'mini-glut' of oil escaping the Gulf, combined with strategic petroleum reserve releases and sluggish demand from China, is creating a near-term oversupply. This is great news for global inflation expectations, but a headache for OPEC+ producers who are meeting this weekend to discuss output targets.

items: What to say in an interview: The collapse in crude to a four-month low shows how quickly geopolitical risk premiums can unwind. With the Strait of Hormuz reopening and US-Iran talks showing real progress, the market is suddenly staring at a supply glut. It's a massive win for central banks fighting inflation.

What to say to colleagues: Watch OPEC+ this weekend. If they agree to hike output targets from August as rumored, they'll be dumping more barrels into an already oversupplied market, which could push Brent below $70.

content.text: 5. Bridgepoint Diversifies with $1.4bn US Real Estate Acquisition

London-listed mid-market private equity firm Bridgepoint agreed to acquire Florida-based Kayne Anderson Real Estate (KARE) for an upfront enterprise value of $1.393 billion. The deal, funded with $759 million in cash and 189 million new Bridgepoint shares, marks Bridgepoint's first major foray into US real estate, adding a fifth investment vertical to its platform.

KARE manages $22 billion in assets, specializing in niche sectors like medical offices, seniors housing, student housing, and light industrial. The acquisition pushes Bridgepoint's total AUM to $117 billion, with real assets (infrastructure and real estate) now representing nearly half of the group's portfolio.

This is a classic scale-and-diversify play for a listed asset manager. Private equity firms are increasingly looking to build 'supermarket' platforms to offer LPs a one-stop-shop across private equity, credit, infrastructure, and real estate. By acquiring a specialist US player, Bridgepoint gains immediate scale in the US and diversifies its recurring fee income, with the deal expected to be immediately accretive to earnings.

items: What to say in an interview: Bridgepoint's acquisition of Kayne Anderson Real Estate is a textbook example of the consolidation happening in the private markets. LPs want to write larger checks to fewer managers, so mid-market PE firms have to scale up or get left behind.

What to say to colleagues: The focus on alternative real estate sectors like medical offices and student housing is smart. These sectors are driven by secular demographic trends rather than the cyclical macro headwinds facing traditional commercial office space.

content.text: 6. Robinhood Eyes 'Hyperscaler' Status with L2 Blockchain Launch

Robinhood (HOOD) shares jumped after Mizuho analyst Dan Dolev raised his price target to $130 from $115, maintaining an Outperform rating. Mizuho argued that Robinhood could become the first true global 'hyperscaler' of online brokerages, leveraging its tech-native platform to expand into highly fragmented markets in Europe and Asia. Coinciding with the upgrade, Robinhood announced the launch of 'Robinhood Chain,' an Ethereum-based Layer-2 blockchain built on Arbitrum Orbit to support tokenized assets.

Robinhood is successfully transitioning from a US-centric 'meme-stock' app into a global, multi-asset financial powerhouse. Its crypto division generated $134 million in Q1 2026, and its launch of tokenized stock derivatives in Europe is paving the way for on-chain finance.

For fintech and equity analysts, Robinhood's tech-first architecture gives it a massive structural advantage over legacy brokerages like Charles Schwab. By building its own L2 blockchain, Robinhood is positioning itself to lead the tokenization of real-world assets (RWA), which could dramatically lower transaction costs and open up global markets that traditional brokers can't easily reach.

items: What to say in an interview: Robinhood's pivot to becoming a global 'hyperscaler' is fascinating. Traditional brokerages are geographically bound and fragmented, but Robinhood is using its tech-native stack and its new Layer-2 blockchain to build a borderless trading ecosystem.

What to say to colleagues: If they can successfully scale tokenized assets globally, they'll leave legacy players like Schwab in the dust. The tokenized stock initiative in Europe is the one to watch—it's a massive regulatory arbitrage play.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: The Great Rotation: Soft Jobs, Cheaper Crude, and a Hawkish Nest

With US markets closed today for the Independence Day holiday, yesterday’s session served as the weekly finale across the pond. On the surface, the S&P 500 looked like a flatline, closing virtually unchanged at 7,483.24. But peel back the skin, and you’ll find a massive cross-asset rotation. The Dow Jones surged 1.1% to a fresh record high of 52,900.07, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq got dragged 0.8% lower to 25,832.67. The message? The market is rejecting 'lazy risk'. The 'buy anything with AI on the tin' trade is getting a harsh reality check, with chipmakers sliding for a second straight day, while capital flows back into broader, value-oriented equities.

The main catalyst was a surprisingly soft US jobs report. Employers added just 57,000 jobs in June—well below the 110,000+ expected by the Street—while the previous two months were revised down by a combined 74,000. While the headline unemployment rate ticked down to 4.2%, the broader picture shows a labor market that is cooling fast. For macro traders, this was a 'bad news is good news' moment: it effectively took any lingering Fed rate-hike fears off the table for the summer, giving a green light to the broader equity market while taking the steam out of tech valuations.

Meanwhile, the energy markets are pricing in a massive peace dividend. The 2026 Iran War, which has dominated macro risk since February, is currently enjoying a 60-day ceasefire signed in mid-June. Technical talks in Qatar are reportedly going well, and the physical market is reacting rapidly: tanker traffic through the critical Strait of Hormuz has quadrupled over the past week, returning to pre-war levels. Brent crude has slid back to around $72 a barrel, almost entirely unwinding the war premium. This is a massive supply-side relief valve for global inflation.

Over here in London, the FTSE 100 is loving it. The blue-chip index hit a four-month high of 10,701 on Friday morning, its highest level since the first week of the war in March. The combination of cheaper crude (which eases corporate cost pressures) and a cooling US economy has put a spring in the step of European equities. Defensive giants like AstraZeneca and consumer staples like Tesco and Sainsbury's have led the charge, proving that when the macro picture gets muddy, the City loves reliable cash flows.

But don't get too comfortable. The Bank of England's resident super-hawk, Catherine Mann, was out on Thursday keeping her trigger finger warm. Speaking at a Natixis event, Mann warned she is ready to vote for an 'activist' rate hike if inflation expectations—which spiked during the war—remain stubborn. The BoE held rates at 3.75% in June in a 7-2 vote, but Mann is clearly the closest to switching. Interestingly, she noted that because markets have recently dialed back their rate-hike expectations, financial conditions have actually loosened. In her eyes, that market relaxation might ironically force the BoE's hand to hike, just to keep the monetary screws tight enough.

items: The Death of Lazy AI Risk: The Nasdaq-Dow divergence shows that investors are demanding actual earnings proof from chipmakers rather than just riding the hype wave.

The Hormuz Peace Dividend: The quadrupling of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is the most important supply-side development of the quarter. If Brent stays near $70, global inflation forecasts will need a serious downward revision.

The 'Activist Hold' Dilemma: Catherine Mann's warning is a masterclass in central bank psychology. If the market assumes the central bank is done hiking and yields fall, they effectively loosen financial conditions themselves—which might force the central bank to hike just to offset the market's optimism. It's a game of chicken between Threadneedle Street and the City.

content.text: The Illusion of the Unicorn: Liquidation Preference

If you spend any time reading about venture capital, growth equity, or tech startups, you will constantly hear about "headline valuations". A company raises £50 million at a £500 million valuation and is crowned a "half-unicorn". Everyone pops the champagne. But in the private markets, a valuation is not just a single number—it is a complex capital structure. And the magic lever that determines who actually gets rich (and who gets wiped out) is the liquidation preference.
What is Liquidation Preference?

When institutional investors put money into private companies, they almost never buy normal common stock (the stuff founders and employees own). Instead, they buy preferred stock. This preferred stock comes with a "liquidation preference"—which is essentially a VIP pass to the front of the buffet line when the company is sold, IPOs, or winds down. It dictates that the investor must get their money back (or a multiple of it) before the common shareholders get a single penny.
There are two main flavours of this preference that you absolutely must know: Non-Participating and Participating.

items: Non-Participating Preferred: The "Either/Or" choice. At exit, the investor can either take their liquidation preference (e.g., get their original investment back) OR convert their shares into common stock and take their pro-rata percentage of the total sale. They will do the math and choose whichever option yields more cash.

Participating Preferred: The "Double Dip". The investor gets their liquidation preference back first, AND then they get to "participate" by taking their pro-rata percentage of whatever money is left over. It is the ultimate downside protection combined with aggressive upside compounding.

content.text: Let's Do the Math

Imagine a startup raises £10 million from a growth equity fund at a £50 million post-money valuation. The fund now owns 20% of the company. The founders and employees own the remaining 80% as common stock. Let's look at how the money is split under two very different exit scenarios.
Scenario A: A Disappointing Exit (The company sells for £15 million)

items: With a 1x Non-Participating Preference: The investor looks at their options. Option 1 is to take their 1x preference (£10 million). Option 2 is to convert to common and take 20% of the £15 million exit (£3 million). Naturally, they take the £10 million. The founders and employees split the remaining £5 million. The investor made their money back, while the founders took a massive haircut.

With a 1x Participating Preference: The investor gets their £10 million back first. This leaves £5 million on the table. Because they "participate", they also take 20% of that remaining £5 million (£1 million). The investor walks away with £11 million, leaving the founders with just £4 million.

content.text: Scenario B: A Home Run Exit (The company sells for £100 million)

items: With a 1x Non-Participating Preference: The investor's 1x preference is £10 million, but their 20% common share of the £100 million exit is £20 million. They convert to common and take the £20 million. The founders take the remaining £80 million. This is the clean, founder-friendly outcome.

With a 1x Participating Preference: The investor gets their £10 million first, leaving £90 million. They then take 20% of that £90 million (£18 million). Total payout to the investor is £28 million, leaving the founders with £72 million. Even in a massive success, the investor "double dipped" to extract an extra £8 million at the founders' expense.

content.text: Why This Matters in Asset Management and Markets

If you are valuing private assets—whether you are in venture capital, growth equity, or a crossover public/private fund—you cannot treat all equity classes the same. When markets turn down, late-stage investors often demand high liquidation preferences (sometimes 1.5x or 2x) to protect their capital. This means the "headline valuation" of a private unicorn is often a complete illusion.

For example, if a company is valued at £1 billion because a late-stage investor put in £100 million at that price, but that investor has a senior liquidation preference, the common stock held by employees is worth far less than the headline price implies. If the company sells for £150 million, the late-stage investor gets their £100 million back, and the rest of the cap table is left fighting over the crumbs. This is why auditors and GPs use complex Option Pricing Models (OPM) or waterfall analyses to value private portfolios for LP reporting, rather than just multiplying the last round's share price by the total share count.
The Common Beginner Mistake

The most common mistake is looking at a private company's cap table and assuming it is a flat pie chart. Beginners think: "If I own 10% of a company, I will get 10% of the exit proceeds." In private markets, the cap table is not a pie; it is a waterfall. You don't know what your equity is worth until you run the exit proceeds through the preference stack from top to bottom.
How to Use This in Interviews

If you are interviewing for a role in private equity, growth equity, or venture capital, you are almost guaranteed to get a waterfall question. A classic test is to see if you can calculate the "crossover point"—the exit valuation at which a non-participating investor decides to convert to common stock. In our example above, the crossover point is £50 million (where 20% of the exit equals the £10 million investment). If you can explain this clearly and walk through the math on a whiteboard without breaking a sweat, you will instantly stand out.
Over a Pint: What to Say at the Pub

"Whenever you hear about a private tech company raising money at a massive headline valuation, remember that it's not a valuation of the company—it's a valuation of the most senior preferred share. If you look at the preference stack, the common equity is probably trading at a 40% discount to that headline price. It's not a billion-dollar company; it's a billion-dollar capital structure."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: The Curse of Dimensionality vs. The Black Box

Imagine you’re running a massive natural gas storage facility in the North Sea, or managing a £50bn pension fund. Every day, you have to make sequential decisions under uncertainty: when to inject or withdraw gas, or how to rebalance your assets to match long-term liabilities. If you go down the classical Dynamic Programming route, you run straight into Bellman’s "curse of dimensionality"—add more than a few state variables (like a multi-tenor forward curve) and your server starts smoking. If you try modern black-box Reinforcement Learning (like PPO), it takes three days to train, and you have absolutely no idea what your risk sensitivities (Greeks) are. If your Chief Risk Officer asks how a 10% parallel shift in the curve affects your strategy, you’re stuck doing "bump-and-revalue"—re-running the entire simulation hundreds of times. It’s the computational equivalent of painting a room by throwing tins of Dulux at the wall.
Enter SNAPO: Smooth Neural Adjoint Policy Optimization

A paper by Dmitri Goloubentsev and Natalija Karpichina (May 2026) introduces SNAPO, a framework that bridges this gap. Instead of treating the simulator as a black box, SNAPO embeds a neural network policy directly inside a known, differentiable simulator. It then replaces hard constraints (like "you cannot hold more than X gas" or "no short-selling") with smooth, continuous mathematical approximations (like softplus functions). Because the entire pipeline—from the neural policy to the simulator to the constraints—is fully differentiable, you can run a single backward pass using reverse-mode automatic differentiation (the adjoint method). This backward pass does two things simultaneously: it updates the neural network's weights to optimize performance, and it calculates the exact sensitivities (Greeks) of your strategy to every single input parameter at zero additional cost.
The Finance Use Case: Pension Fund ALM

In pension fund Asset-Liability Management (ALM), you have a multi-asset portfolio and complex liabilities that depend on inflation, interest rates, and longevity. You want a neural network to decide the asset allocation every month. With SNAPO, you train this policy directly inside a differentiable ALM simulator. The same backward pass that updates the neural network also gives you the exact sensitivities of your optimal policy to all risk factors (e.g., interest rate shifts at 50 different maturities). Instead of bumping each rate one by one and re-running the simulation (bump-and-revalue), you get all 50 sensitivities instantly. The authors demonstrate a 6.5x to 200x speedup in sensitivity calculations over traditional methods, scaling directly with the number of risk factors.
A Mini Technical Blueprint
Here is a simplified PyTorch-style blueprint of how you can build a differentiable simulator with a neural policy and smooth constraints to get instant sensitivities:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class StoragePolicy(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(2, 16),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(16, 1),
            nn.Tanh() # Action between -1 (withdraw) and 1 (inject)
        )
    def forward(self, state):
        return self.net(state)

def step_simulator(inventory, price, action, capacity, max_rate):
    flow = action * max_rate
    next_inventory = inventory + flow
    
    # Smooth constraints: softplus acts as a smooth penalty
    over_capacity_penalty = torch.log(1 + torch.exp(next_inventory - capacity))
    under_zero_penalty = torch.log(1 + torch.exp(-next_inventory))
    penalty = 1000.0 * (over_capacity_penalty + under_zero_penalty)
    
    # Smoothly clamp inventory for the next step
    next_inventory_clamped = torch.sigmoid((next_inventory - capacity/2) / 10) * capacity
    profit = -flow * price - penalty
    return next_inventory_clamped, profit

policy = StoragePolicy()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(policy.parameters(), lr=0.01)

# Input parameters (e.g., forward curve prices)
prices = torch.tensor([2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 2.5], requires_grad=True)
inventory = torch.tensor(10.0)

total_profit = 0.0
for t in range(len(prices)):
    state = torch.stack([inventory, prices[t]])
    action = policy(state)
    inventory, profit = step_simulator(inventory, prices[t], action, 100.0, 10.0)
    total_profit += profit

loss = -total_profit
loss.backward() # The magic: computes policy grads AND input sensitivities

optimizer.step() # Updates policy weights
price_sensitivities = prices.grad # Instant Greeks!
The Pub / Interview Conversation Starter

If you want to sound like the smartest quant in the room, bring this up when someone mentions using Reinforcement Learning for portfolio optimization or execution. You can say: "The problem with standard RL in production is that it's a black box—you can't get risk sensitivities without doing incredibly slow bump-and-revalue. But if you build a differentiable simulator and smooth out the hard constraints, you can use adjoint automatic differentiation—like the SNAPO framework—to train the policy and get all your Greeks in a single backward pass. It basically runs backprop all the way through the simulator, giving you exact sensitivities to hundreds of risk factors for free."
The Catch

Of course, there is no free lunch in the City. SNAPO has three main limitations. First, you need a fully differentiable simulator. If your simulation relies on discrete logic, lookup tables, or external black-box APIs that you can't backprop through, you're out of luck. Second, the "smooth constraint bias" means that by replacing hard boundaries with soft penalties, your model might slightly violate constraints in extreme scenarios, requiring careful tuning of the penalty parameters. Finally, because you are optimizing a neural network inside a simulator, the loss landscape is highly non-convex, meaning you are still at the mercy of your random seed and local minima.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: The Paper: The Fragility of Semi-Liquid Private Credit Funds

Private credit has been the undisputed darling of the City for years. But as institutional capital got crowded, the big managers turned to the holy grail of asset management: "democratisation"—marketing private debt to retail investors and wealth management channels. To do this, they packaged illiquid middle-market loans into "semi-liquid" vehicles like Business Development Companies (BDCs) and interval funds, which now manage over $300 billion. The pitch? You get the juicy private credit yield, but with the comfort of quarterly redemptions (usually capped at 5% of NAV). Sounds like a free lunch, right? Well, a brand-new NBER working paper by Chuck Fang, Itay Goldstein, and Yao Zeng says the lunch is actually a ticking liquidity timebomb.
Why This One Matters

This paper is the first major academic takedown of the semi-liquid private credit promise. It shows that these funds are performing classic "liquidity transformation"—holding highly illiquid assets while promising regular cash outs—and that the 5% quarterly gates do not actually stop runs. Instead, they just slow them down while shifting the liquidation and leverage costs onto the investors who stay behind. Even better, the authors use a brilliant, highly topical trigger to prove their point: the recent software/SaaS markdown driven by the rise of AI agents.
The Core Argument: Stale NAVs and the Leverage Loop

The plumbing of a semi-liquid BDC is surprisingly fragile. The authors analyse regulatory filings for 59 semi-liquid BDCs and find that their cash buffers are tiny—averaging just 5% of net assets. That means a single quarter of maximum redemptions wipes out all their cash. When the redemptions keep coming, what do they do? They cannot easily sell mid-market loans, which are highly illiquid and unrated. Instead, they do three things: sell what they can, draw down on external credit lines (ramping up leverage), and delay payments via "repurchases payable".

This creates what economists call "strategic complementarity"—or in plain English, a massive first-mover advantage. Because private credit loans are valued using stale or inflated NAVs that adjust slowly to market realities, the investors who redeem first get to exit at an artificially high price. The investors who stay behind are left holding a fund that is now highly leveraged, has dumped its most liquid assets, and is saddled with the borrowing costs. It is a textbook run incentive, dressed up in a shiny retail wrapper.
The AI/SaaS Natural Experiment

How do you prove this run behaviour actually happens in a market where loans do not trade? The authors look at the recent "software crisis" of late 2025 and early 2026. Software and SaaS companies make up a massive chunk of private credit—about 19% of all middle-market loans. When rapid advancements in AI agents threatened to replace traditional SaaS business models, it triggered a wave of loan markdowns. Because a BDC's exposure to software is public knowledge, investors used it as a signal. BDCs with high software exposure saw immediate, massive spikes in redemption requests, proving that public bad news triggers run-like behaviour even through quarterly gates.

"Our evidence suggests that quarterly gates and redemption caps do not eliminate run-like fragility in semi-liquid private credit funds, raising cautions about expanding retail access to private credit markets."
What to Skim vs. What to Read

items: Read: The Introduction (Section 1) for the high-level thesis and the policy implications.
Read: Section 5 (Software exposure and BDC flows) to see how they link the AI/SaaS disruption directly to fund runs. It is a brilliant piece of empirical work.
Skim: The heavy structural model equations in Sections 3 and 4, unless you really want to lose your Friday afternoon to Greek letters.

content.text: How to Use This at Work (or in the Pub)

If you are in asset management, wealth management, or private debt, this is essential ammunition. The industry is already fighting back—private debt giant Cliffwater released a sharp critique of the paper, calling it "useful red meat for the press" but flawed in its methodology. This sets up a classic battle between academic purists and the private credit lobby.

At your next team meeting or over a pint, you can sound like the smartest person in the room by saying: "The NBER paper on semi-liquid private credit is a massive warning shot. It proves that the 5% quarterly gate does not stop runs; it just subsidises the first movers who exit at stale NAVs, leaving the remaining investors holding a highly leveraged, illiquid portfolio. And using the SaaS AI markdown as the empirical proof of run behaviour is incredibly clever."

content.text: The Shirky Principle: Why some problems are too profitable to fix

Have you ever sat in a meeting, staring at a mind-numbingly inefficient process—say, a manual spreadsheet reconciliation that takes three people four days every month—and wondered, "Why on earth haven’t we automated this yet?" You know a basic Python script or a modern SaaS tool could do it in seconds. You’ve probably even suggested it, only to be met with a wall of vague, bureaucratic pushback about "operational risk," "governance," or "legacy integration."

It’s easy to chalk this up to standard corporate incompetence. But the real culprit is usually something far more logical: The Shirky Principle. Coined by internet theorist Clay Shirky and popularised by Kevin Kelly, the principle states: "Institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution".

This isn’t a conspiracy theory; it’s just rational self-preservation. If your entire job, department budget, or consulting retainer is predicated on "managing" a complex, messy problem, you have a massive, unspoken incentive to ensure that problem never actually gets solved.
The billable hour and the empire builders

In the City, the Shirky Principle is everywhere. Take external consulting. If a major advisory firm is billing £250,000 a month to "oversee the transition" of a legacy core banking system, they are not incentivised to deliver a simple, elegant solution that wraps up in three weeks. They are incentivised to find "unexpected complexities" that require a phase two, a phase three, and a team of twenty junior consultants to manage.

Or look internally at corporate "empire building." A middle manager’s status, pay, and promotion prospects in an investment bank or asset manager are often tied directly to their headcount. If a manager has a team of 30 people manually processing trade breaks, automating that process down to a team of two is a career catastrophe. They lose their empire. Consequently, they will find every reason under the sun why the manual process is "critical for risk management".
How to use this at work
Once you understand the Shirky Principle, you stop trying to win arguments with pure logic. If you are pitching a new tool, an AI automation, or a process overhaul, you need to change your strategy:

items: Identify the 'Problem Owner': Before you pitch an elegant solution, ask yourself: Who loses out if this problem disappears? Whose headcount, budget, or billable hours are threatened?

Reframe the Pitch: Never tell an empire builder that your tool will 'eliminate' their team's workload. Instead, frame it as a tool that 'unlocks capacity' for them to tackle a much bigger, more prestigious problem. You aren't shrinking their empire; you're giving them higher-quality territory to rule.

Align the Incentives: If you're hiring external vendors or consultants, structure contracts around outcomes (e.g., a fixed fee for a fully automated system) rather than time-and-materials. If you pay them by the hour to manage a mess, don't be surprised when the mess gets bigger.

content.text: One line to remember
"If you want to know why a stupid corporate problem won't go away, look at who gets paid to manage it."
